screens.title: Final Examination and Answer Key
screens.subtitle: Review, diagnosis, and a model solution that ties together the course's core ROS patterns

narration.text: This final chapter bundles testing, diagnosis, and a model architecture so you can prove you understand ROS fundamentals. We'll walk through the exam structure — multiple choice, short answers, code analysis, and a design task — and then review each answer with the reasoning behind it. That reasoning is the skill you need: not just memorizing commands, but knowing when to use topics, services, actions, parameters, and launch files. For example, the exam highlights that topics are best for continuous sensor streams while services are for discrete requests; understanding that distinction helps you design robust systems. We'll also inspect common bugs shown in the code questions: forgetting to keep a node alive, placing parameters in the wrong scope in a launch file, and ignoring action preemption. Finally, the model smart-home solution consolidates nodes, topics, an action server, and a simple alert service to show how pieces fit together. By the end you should be able to explain each answer, recognize the common pitfalls, and apply these patterns to your own robot projects. Where do you want to focus first: communication primitives, debugging, or system design?

narration.text: These objectives emphasize transferable skills you will need beyond the exam. First, interpret system graphs and visualization tools to verify that nodes are connected correctly. For example, rqt_graph helps you confirm that a publisher and subscriber share a topic name and that the message types match. Second, use the Parameter Server and launch files to configure robotic behavior without changing code; practical examples include swapping PID gains or adjusting patrol intervals through YAML-loaded parameters. Third, plan for concurrency and cancellation: actions provide asynchronous goals with feedback and allow preemption, so servers must check for cancellation requests. Finally, practice reading multi-language systems: a Python publisher and C++ subscriber must share the same generated message type and the same exact topic name. Checking these things is how you prevent the most common cross-language communication failures. Each of these skills lets you debug faster and design more resilient systems for both simulation and hardware.

screens.title: What is ROS and the role of the ROS Master?
screens.subtitle: Definitions, responsibilities, and a common misconception

narration.text: Start by anchoring the basic definition you saw on the exam. ROS is a middleware framework that provides communication infrastructure for robot components. That means ROS is the plumbing: it gives named topics, services, parameters, and a registry that helps nodes find each other. The ROS Master is a registry service that keeps track of who provides which topics and services and how names map to nodes. It does not forward every message; it enables publishers and subscribers to locate each other so they can talk directly when possible. A common misconception is to treat ROS as a real-time operating system or to assume the Master routes every message like a broker. The correct view is that the Master facilitates discovery and name registration. For example, when a camera node registers a publisher for /camera/image_raw, the Master records that information. When a GUI subscribes, the Master tells the two processes how to connect. This matters in practice because if the Master is not running, discovery fails and nodes cannot find topics, even though individual processes might still be alive. Key takeaway: ROS handles communication patterns and discovery, not low-level device drivers or deterministic real-time scheduling. A good check after starting roscore is to run rqt_graph and confirm that nodes have been registered; if they are missing, check that each node used a unique name and that the Master is reachable.

keyIdea.title: ROS vs an OS
keyIdea.text: ROS is middleware for discovery and messaging; the ROS Master is a registry that connects publishers and subscribers, not a message broker.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › What is ROS?
Core Concept

ROS as middleware

ROS provides naming, discovery, and communication channels for distributed robot software. The Master registers node names, topics, and services.

Definition

Middleware framework that provides communication infrastructure for robots.

Misconception

ROS is not a real-time OS and the Master does not forward every message; it manages discovery and registration.

Concrete example

A camera node registers /camera/image_raw with the Master; when a display node subscribes, the Master supplies connection info so the two can communicate.

Key Takeaway

Think discovery and naming first. If nodes are missing in rqt_graph, check roscore and node names.

Quick checklist
  • Is roscore running? Without it, discovery fails.
  • Do nodes use unique names or anonymous=True where needed?
  • Use rqt_graph to confirm registrations and connections.
Why this matters

Discovery problems look like communication failures. Fix the registry issues before chasing message-handling bugs.

screens.title: Topics, Services, and Actions — choosing the right primitive
screens.subtitle: Behavior, timing, and example use cases

narration.text: Understanding the practical difference between topics, services, and actions is central to the exam and to good system design. A topic is a one-way, asynchronous channel: publishers stream messages and subscribers receive them without a direct reply. Use topics for continuous data like sensor streams or status broadcasts — the camera image stream is a textbook example. A service is synchronous and blocking: a client sends a request and waits for a response. Use services for discrete queries such as asking for a battery level or toggling a device. An action is an asynchronous goal-based interface that provides feedback and can be preempted; it’s designed for long-running processes where you want progress updates and the ability to cancel. For instance, an inspection routine that takes several seconds and reports percent-complete fits an action. A common misconception is to overuse services for tasks that are long-running; that leads to blocking behaviour that can stall the system. Another mistake is to try to force feedback over a service instead of using an action. When choosing between them, ask: is this a stream, a quick request, or a goal with progress and cancellation? That simple question will guide the right selection for robust behavior.

keyIdea.title: Selection rule
keyIdea.text: Ask: stream, one-time request, or cancellable long goal? Use topics for streams, services for immediate request-response, and actions for long goals with feedback.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Topics vs Services vs Actions
Comparison
Topic — continuous stream

One-way, asynchronous. Example: camera publishes images on /camera/image_raw continuously.

Service — request/response

Synchronous, blocking. Example: /get_battery_level returns current charge on demand.

Action — goal with feedback

Asynchronous goal, provides feedback and can be canceled. Example: /inspect_area action for camera inspection with progress updates.

Common mistake

Using a service for long-running tasks instead of an action causes blocking and poor feedback.

Decision checklist
  1. If data is continuous and many nodes may consume it, choose a topic.
  2. If the interaction is a quick query with an immediate answer, choose a service.
  3. If the task runs for a while and needs feedback or cancellation, choose an action.
Concrete example
Patrol robot: motion sensor publishes boolean on /motion (topic). When true, patrol_controller sends a goal to /inspect_area (action) so camera_node can stream high-res images for a fixed interval. The alert path uses a service to log or notify on demand.

screens.title: The ROS Parameter Server and launch files
screens.subtitle: How runtime configuration and launch scoping help reuse code

narration.text: Parameters let you separate configuration from code. The Parameter Server is a shared key-value store started with roscore that nodes can read from and write to. Use it to load values like patrol intervals, PID gains, or house names from YAML at launch time rather than hard-coding them. Launch files let you start multiple nodes and set parameters together. They also control the scope of parameters: a param inside a node tag becomes private to that node if you intend it to be so. A common exam bug illustrated placing outside the node tag; that makes it global rather than private. For practical use, load configuration with a launch file that sets /patrol_interval and /house_name and then starts sensor and controller nodes. When testing, change the YAML parameter and relaunch without modifying source code. Remember to check parameter scope and whether you meant a private or global name. Also ensure your launch tags are correctly nested; misplacing a param can silently configure the wrong part of your system. In short: parameters and launch files make systems configurable and reusable; pay attention to where parameters live so the right node reads them.

keyIdea.title: Configure, don't compile
keyIdea.text: Use the Parameter Server and launch files to tune behavior at runtime and avoid scattering constants in code.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Parameters & Launch
Process Flow
1
Start roscore
Parameter Server becomes available for storing config values.
2
Launch file sets params
Launch loads YAML or sets tags to configure nodes at startup.
3
Nodes read parameters
Nodes fetch values from the Parameter Server at runtime to vary behavior without code changes.
Key Takeaway

Place params where you intend them to live: inside a node tag for private params, globally when you want system-wide values.

Concrete example & fix
The buggy launch file placed outside the node. To make it a private parameter for the node, move the param inside the node block so it configures that node only.
Why this matters: scoping mistakes lead to unexpected values and make debugging harder when many nodes share similar names or parameters.

screens.title: rosbag vs rostopic — recording and playback
screens.subtitle: Capture real data for debugging and offline analysis

narration.text: Recording topic data is an essential debugging and research tool. The exam points out that rosbag record is the correct command to record topic traffic for later playback. rosbag captures the actual messages on topics to a file that you can replay to reproduce behavior, test algorithms offline, or feed recorded sensor streams into a simulation. rostopic record is not the correct command in this exam — the intended tool is rosbag record. A practical example: if your patrol robot produced a burst of motion events and you want to analyze camera frames and motion timestamps together, start rosbag record for /camera/image_raw and /motion, then replay them with rosbag play to reproduce the sequence. Common mistakes include recording the wrong topics or forgetting to set an adequate queue_size when publishing, which can drop messages before recording. Also check that the topics are spelled exactly: a leading slash changes the effective name. Use rosbag to create reproducible test data that helps you isolate perception and control bugs without running hardware every time. rosbag vs rostopic — recording and playback means rosbag record captures topic traffic to recreate and analyze real robot runs offline for debugging and testing.. In practical terms, capture real data for debugging and offline analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use rosbag for reproducibility
keyIdea.text: rosbag record captures topic traffic to recreate and analyze real robot runs offline for debugging and testing.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › rosbag Recording
Definition

rosbag record

Capture topic messages to a file for later playback. Useful for debugging, testing, and offline analysis.

Example
Record a camera and motion stream: rosbag record /camera/image_raw /motion. Later, replay with rosbag play to reproduce timings.
Common Mistake

Recording the wrong topic name or forgetting to set publisher queue sizes can lead to lost data in the bag file.

Practical tip

When recording multi-topic sessions, include only the topics you need to keep bag size manageable. Use tools to inspect bag contents and timestamps before replaying.

Rosbag helps you make experiments reproducible and decouple debugging from hardware availability.

screens.title: Diagnosing a publisher/subscriber mismatch
screens.subtitle: Five common causes when a subscriber sees no messages

narration.text: When a subscriber does not receive messages despite using the same topic name, the exam lists several realistic causes and fixes. First, ensure the development environment is sourced: forgetting to source devel/setup. bash can prevent nodes from finding message definitions and packages. Second, confirm that the message types match exactly and are generated from the same package; mismatched generated message hashes stop communication even if the. msg files look identical. Third, verify the topic names are identical, including leading slashes; /robot_news and robot_news are distinct topics. Fourth, check that nodes are actually spinning: in Python, missing a call to keep the node alive stops callbacks from running. Fifth, make sure the executable and node names in launch or rosrun are correct so the intended node runs. Another practical issue is queue_size misconfiguration or network/firewall issues in distributed setups. The right debugging order is: check roscore and rqt_graph for registrations, confirm topic spelling and message types, ensure devel was sourced, and finally add logs or increase queue sizes to reveal dropped messages. This stepwise approach prevents wild code changes and speeds resolution.

keyIdea.title: Debugging checklist
keyIdea.text: Check sourcing, message types, exact topic names, spinning, and correct executables in that order to find missed messages quickly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Publisher/Subscriber Mismatch
Common Causes
  1. devel/setup.bash not sourced — message types not found.
  2. Message definitions differ — generated types mismatch.
  3. Topic name mismatch — leading slash or typo.
  4. Node not spinning — callbacks never executed.
  5. Wrong executable or launch configuration.
Step-by-step fix
1) Confirm roscore is running and inspect rqt_graph. 2) Use rostopic list and rostopic type to verify topic names and types. 3) Source your workspace and rebuild message packages if needed. 4) Add logging and verify nodes call spin. 5) Check launch file names and remaps.
Key Takeaway

Work from discovery to message format to runtime behavior; that order finds root causes faster than random edits.

screens.title: rospy subscriber without spin — the missing loop
screens.subtitle: Why the callback never runs and how to fix it

narration.text: This code-analysis question surfaces a simple but common Python mistake: creating a subscriber and then exiting the script. The example subscribes to /chatter and defines a callback that prints the received data, but it omits the mechanism that keeps the node alive and processing callbacks. In rospy, rospy. spin() hands control to the ROS callback system so that your callback functions are invoked when messages arrive. Without it, the script finishes immediately and the subscriber never processes messages. A robust fix is to add rospy. spin() at the end and, as a best practice, wrap node setup in a guard block so the module can be imported without side effects. For example, initialize the node and subscriber inside if name == 'main': and then call rospy. spin(). This pattern avoids unexpected behavior when unit testing or importing the module. Also consider adding logging and exception handling to fail gracefully if roscore is not available. Common misconceptions are thinking that Subscriber creation implicitly starts a loop or that while True with sleep is necessary; neither is required if you use rospy. spin(). The takeaway: keep nodes alive to process callbacks — forgetting spin is a simple runtime trap.

keyIdea.title: Keep the node alive
keyIdea.text: Add rospy.spin() and use the __main__ guard so subscribers can process callbacks and your module is import-safe.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › rospy.spin()
Problem
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

def callback(msg):
    print(msg.data)

rospy.init_node('listener')
sub = rospy.Subscriber('/chatter', String, callback)
This node creates the subscriber but exits immediately because there is no call to keep the process alive.
Corrected version
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

def callback(msg):
    print(msg.data)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    rospy.init_node('listener')
    sub = rospy.Subscriber('/chatter', String, callback)
    rospy.spin()
Key Takeaway

rospy.spin() or an equivalent loop is required so callbacks can run; use the __main__ guard for safe imports.

screens.title: Launch file bug and remapping
screens.subtitle: Scope params correctly and use <remap> for names when needed

narration.text: Launch files orchestrate multiple nodes and set parameters, but small structural mistakes can change system behavior. The exam example showed a tag placed outside a, which makes the parameter global rather than private to that node. If the intent is to pass a max_speed private to my_node, place the inside that node tag so the node reads its own private parameter. Another launch feature your exam covered is, which redirects topic or service names to alternate names; this is useful for testing or when integrating components that expect different names. For example, if a package publishes to /camera but a consumer expects /front_camera, use in the launch. A common misconception is that remap changes the node's code; it only adjusts the name bindings at runtime. Also check that Python nodes are executable and have a proper shebang. Finally, always test launch files by running roslaunch and inspecting rqt_graph to verify that parameters, remaps, and nodes are applied as intended. Thoughtful launch structure keeps configuration separate from code and simplifies testing across robots and simulations. Launch file bug and remapping means keep parameters and remaps in the intended scope and verify behavior with rqt_graph after launching.. In practical terms, scope params correctly and use <remap> for names when needed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Launch hygiene
keyIdea.text: Keep parameters and remaps in the intended scope and verify behavior with rqt_graph after launching.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Launch File Best Practices
Bug example
<launch>
  <node pkg="my_pkg" type="my_node.py" name="my_node" />
  <param name="max_speed" value="1.5" />
</launch>

Fix: move the param inside the node block so it is private to my_node.
Make parameters private when they are node-specific and global when they are shared. Always test the launch outcome with rqt_graph and rostopic list.
Remap usage
Use <remap from="/old_name" to="/new_name" /> inside a node to redirect names without changing source code. This is ideal for experimentation or integrating modules with different name conventions.
Key Takeaway

Launch files are powerful: design them to express configuration and mappings so your code remains portable.

screens.title: Action server pattern: feedback and preemption
screens.subtitle: Designing an action server that respects cancellation requests

narration.text: Action servers are designed for long-running goals where clients need feedback and the option to cancel. The exam's C++ snippet loops to publish feedback and then sets success without checking for preemption. This is a critical bug: if the client cancels, the server should honor that request and set the goal as preempted rather than succeed. The fix is to check _as. isPreemptRequested() inside the loop, call _as. setPreempted() and return when cancellation is requested. Also avoid tight loops that run as fast as possible — add a ros::Rate or sleep to give other threads time and to provide realistic progress updates. For example, in a ten-step inspection, check for preemption each iteration, publish feedback. percentage, sleep for a small interval, and if preempted, set preempted and exit. Also ensure the server publishes meaningful feedback and a clear result structure so the client can react. Misconceptions include treating actions as services with simple replies; actions are a richer protocol and need explicit management of state and cancellation. Always write action servers defensively to allow responsive cancellation and predictable results. Action server pattern: feedback and preemption means action servers must check for preempt requests and respond quickly; otherwise clients cannot reliably cancel goals.. In practical terms, designing an action server that respects cancellation requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Respect cancellation
keyIdea.text: Action servers must check for preempt requests and respond quickly; otherwise clients cannot reliably cancel goals.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Action Server Design
Problematic snippet
for (int i = 0; i < goal->count; ++i) {
    my_pkg::MyActionFeedback feedback;
    feedback.percentage = float(i) / goal->count;
    _as.publishFeedback(feedback);
}
_as.setSucceeded(result);
This loop never checks for preemption and will always report success even if the client cancels the goal.
Corrected approach
for (int i = 0; i < goal->count; ++i) {
    if (_as.isPreemptRequested()) {
        _as.setPreempted();
        return;
    }
    my_pkg::MyActionFeedback feedback;
    feedback.percentage = float(i) / goal->count;
    _as.publishFeedback(feedback);
    ros::Duration(0.1).sleep();
}
_as.setSucceeded(result);
Pro Tip

Give frequent, meaningful feedback and check preemption often so clients can cancel promptly and the system remains responsive.

screens.title: Smart-home patrol system — node design and message flows
screens.subtitle: A concrete architecture that meets the practical problem requirements

narration.text: The practical problem asks you to design a smart-home robot that patrols and reports sensor readings. The provided model maps each requirement to a node and communication channel. sensor_publisher provides three topics: /temperature with Float64 for periodic temperature readings, /motion with Bool for motion events, and /camera/image_raw for images. patrol_controller subscribes to /motion and, when motion is true, sends a goal to /inspect_area on camera_node; it also calls the /send_alert service on alert_service to notify or log the event. camera_node provides the /inspect_area action server. When a goal arrives, it publishes high-resolution images on /camera/image_raw for ten seconds and sends progress feedback. alert_service implements /send_alert to log messages or trigger notifications. dashboard subscribes to the three sensor topics to display data. Parameters like /house_name, /patrol_interval, and /alert_threshold_temp are set via launch file so you can tune behavior without changing code. The launch file smart_home. launch starts all nodes and sets parameters. This architecture demonstrates clear separation of concerns, predictable topic names, and the correct use of actions for long-running inspection tasks. The exam model code implements these nodes in Python and provides a launch file you can run to verify behavior.

keyIdea.title: Architecture mapping
keyIdea.text: Map sensors to publishers, events to topics, discrete notifications to services, and long inspections to actions; configure via parameters and launch files.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Smart-home Architecture
System Components
sensor_publisher
Publishes /temperature (Float64), /motion (Bool), /camera/image_raw (Image).
patrol_controller
Subscribes to /motion, sends goals to /inspect_area, and calls /send_alert when motion occurs.
camera_node
Hosts an action server /inspect_area and publishes higher-resolution images during inspection.
alert_service
Provides /send_alert service to log alerts when called by patrol_controller.
Key Takeaway

Design each node with a single responsibility and pick the communication primitive that matches the interaction pattern.

Launch & Parameters
smart_home.launch sets /house_name, /patrol_interval, and /alert_threshold_temp, then starts all nodes. Tuning these values at launch lets you reuse the code across environments.
This architecture mirrors the exam answer and is ready to run after marking executables and message definitions correctly.

screens.title: Exam strategy and common pitfalls
screens.subtitle: How to approach questions and spot distractors

narration.text: Approaching the exam effectively means reading questions for intent and using simple checks to eliminate distractors. For multiple-choice items, confirm that the answer matches both the definition and the intended use case. For instance, when asked which mechanism streams continuous sensor data, validate whether streaming and multiple listeners are implied — that points to topics. In code analysis, look for missing lifecycle calls, incorrect scoping, or absent error checks; these are common exam targets. For debugging questions, adopt a reproducible procedure: verify roscore, inspect the graph, confirm topic names and message types, then check runtime behaviors like spinning and queue sizes. In design problems, map each requirement to a node and a communication primitive, then show how parameters and the launch file bind everything together. Watch for traps: terms like "real-time OS" or claims that the Master forwards messages are common distractors. Lastly, practice explaining your reasoning out loud: stating why other choices are wrong often reveals the right option. Use the exam as an opportunity to demonstrate both factual knowledge and practical debugging instincts — that combination is what employers and projects need.

keyIdea.title: Answer with reasoning
keyIdea.text: Always pair an asserted fact with a practical check or reproduction step so you can justify why an answer is correct.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Exam Strategy
Multiple-choice tactics
  • Match definitions to use cases, not just short descriptions.
  • Eliminate distractors that state partial truths out of context.
  • Prefer the answer that aligns with the communication pattern and runtime behavior.
Code & design tactics

For code, run through lifecycle expectations: is the node kept alive, are callbacks processed, are preemption checks present? For designs, map requirements directly to nodes and primitives and show a launch file to tie them together.

A calm, stepwise approach beats guesswork when time is limited.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas that explain most exam answers

narration.text: Summarizing the chapter into three compact ideas helps you recall the essential principles under test conditions. First, communication primitives: topics are for streams, services for synchronous queries, and actions for long-running goals with feedback and cancellation. Knowing this distinction answers many exam and design questions. Second, discovery and configuration: the ROS Master handles discovery and the Parameter Server plus launch files handle runtime configuration; both must be working and properly scoped for systems to behave as expected. Third, defensive node design: keep nodes alive to process callbacks, check for action preemption, and verify message type and exact topic name matches across languages. These three concepts explain most correct answers, point directly to common bugs, and guide robust system design. Keep these in mind as short checks when you encounter an unfamiliar question: ask which primitive fits the pattern, whether discovery or configuration might be failing, and whether the node lifecycle is handled correctly.

keyIdea.title: Three cornerstones
keyIdea.text: Communications, discovery/configuration, and defensive node design cover the majority of exam reasoning and practical fixes.

Choose topics for streams, services for requests, and actions for cancellable goals with feedback.
Discovery & config

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Short reminders to carry forward after the exam

narration.text: As you finish the course and review the exam answers, keep three practical reminders in mind. First, reproduce problems: use rosbag play and rostopic tools to recreate and inspect system behavior offline. Second, prefer clear names and parameter scoping in launch files so your systems remain predictable across runs and robots. Third, practice writing small, defensive nodes that handle lifecycle events and cancellations gracefully; these are the scripts that survive the most painful debugging sessions. The course conclusion also suggested next steps: learning ROS 2, exploring advanced packages like MoveIt or the Navigation Stack, and applying these fundamentals to a real robot. But before that, ensure you can explain why each exam choice is correct and how the code changes fix the observed failures. That explanation is the real certification of understanding. Now, take a moment to test yourself by explaining one answer aloud and then implementing the quick fix in your workspace.

keyIdea.title: Three practical reminders
keyIdea.text: Reproduce issues with recorded data, use clear launch scoping, and write defensive node code that handles lifecycle events.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › What to Remember
Reproduce issues
Use rosbag to capture and replay data so debugging does not depend on live hardware.
Scope configs
Place parameters correctly in launch files to avoid surprising global overrides.
Defensive code
Keep nodes alive, check preemption, and ensure message/type/name consistency across languages.
Parting thought

Understanding the why behind each answer makes you a better practitioner — not just someone who passes the test.
